name: MyoAdapt
tagline: An adaptive training app that adjusts strength programming based on logged performance and recovery.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Adaptive training apps are mostly a logging table plus an opinionated progression rule, and both of those are well within one-shot range. An agent can give you sets, reps, RPE, e1RM estimates, and a rule that bumps or drops load based on last session's performance, running entirely on your phone. What it cannot give you is the part that makes these products feel smart: a programming model tuned against thousands of real lifters, plus the UI discipline to be usable with sweaty hands between sets. If the app leans on wearable or EMG data, that integration is the real work and it is not a one-sitting job. Treat the DIY version as a very good logbook that happens to do arithmetic for you.
coreLoopDIY: A local-first PWA that stores your lifts, estimates e1RM, and prescribes next session's load from simple autoregulation rules you can edit.
requirements: A phone browser that supports installable PWAs
A willingness to pick your own progression rules instead of trusting someone else's model
Optional: manual entry for sleep or soreness if you want the recovery input
whatYouLose: A progression model validated on a real population instead of whatever heuristic you typed in
Any wearable, heart rate, or sensor integration
Exercise library with demo videos and substitution logic
Polished between-sets UX: rest timers, big tap targets, one-handed logging
Cross device sync and backup unless you bolt on your own
moatNotes: The programming logic is the asset, and it only gets better with a user base logging against it. A solo build cannot bootstrap that.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because most people do not want to decide what weight to put on the bar, and a paid app sells that decision with enough confidence that you stop second guessing it. A homemade tracker makes you both the lifter and the programmer, which is exactly the job you were trying to outsource. The subscription is also a commitment device: paying for it is part of why you open it on a Tuesday in February.
notes: Logging is trivial, programming is not. Build it if you already know what progression scheme you want.
prompt:
Build a local-first adaptive strength training tracker as an installable PWA. Empty folder, no backend.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + React + TypeScript
- Dexie (IndexedDB) for all storage, single user, no accounts
- Tailwind for styling, dark by default
- vite-plugin-pwa for offline install, service worker precaching the whole app shell

Data model:
- exercises: id, name, category, defaultUnit (kg or lb)
- workouts: id, date, notes, readiness (1 to 5, optional)
- sets: id, workoutId, exerciseId, weight, reps, rpe (optional), isWarmup

Features that are in scope:
1. Today view: start a workout, pick exercises, log sets with big touch targets. Weight and reps use steppers, not tiny text inputs. Assume one hand and bad lighting.
2. Rest timer that starts automatically after a logged set, configurable per exercise, visible without navigating away.
3. e1RM per set using Epley, charted per exercise over time.
4. Autoregulation engine in src/lib/progression.ts: a pure function that takes exercise history plus today's readiness and returns a suggested weight and rep target. Ship two swappable strategies, linear progression and RPE-based (target RPE 8, adjust load by comparing last session's actual RPE). Make the strategy selectable per exercise in settings. Comment the formulas clearly so they can be edited.
5. History view: list of past workouts, tap to expand sets, edit or delete.
6. Export and import the whole database as JSON from a settings screen. This is the only backup mechanism.

Out of scope, do not build:
- Accounts, login, cloud sync, telemetry, analytics of any kind
- Wearable, Apple Health, or Google Fit integration
- Exercise demo videos or an exercise encyclopedia
- Social feed, sharing, leaderboards

Seed the exercise table with about 20 common barbell, dumbbell, and machine movements. No .env is needed because nothing leaves the device; if you add one later, keep secrets there and gitignore it.

Write a README that states plainly: the progression rules are hand written heuristics, not validated science, and the user should edit progression.ts to match their own program.
